definition: In mathematics (in particular, functional analysis), convolution is a mathematical operation on two functions f {\displaystyle f} and g {\displaystyle g} that produces a third function f ∗ g {\displaystyle f*g} , as the integral of the product of the two functions after one is reflected about the y-axis and shifted.
details: The term convolution refers to both the resulting function and to the process of computing it. The integral is evaluated for all values of shift, producing the convolution function. The choice of which function is reflected and shifted before the integral does not change the integral result (see commutativity). Graphically, it expresses how the 'shape' of one function is modified by the other. Some features of convolution are similar to cross-correlation: for real-valued functions, of a continuous or discrete variable, convolution f ∗ g {\displaystyle f*g} differs from cross-correlation f ⋆ g {\displaystyle f\star g} only in that either f ( x ) {\displaystyle f(x)} or g ( x ) {\displaystyle g(x)} is reflected about the y-axis in convolution; thus it is a cross-correlation of g ( − x ) {\displaystyle g(-x)} and f ( x ) {\displaystyle f(x)} , or f ( − x ) {\displaystyle f(-x)} and g ( x ) {\displaystyle g(x)} . For complex-valued functions, the cross-correlation operator is the adjoint of the convolution operator. Convolution has applications that include probability, statistics, acoustics, spectroscopy, signal processing and image processing, computer vision and human vision, geophy

explainer.lead: Convolution combines two functions by sliding a reflected version of one across the other and measuring their product at every position. It shows how one function reshapes another, and it appears in fields from statistics and signal processing to image processing and computer vision.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sliding one patterned transparent sheet over another and checking how much they overlap at each position. You flip one sheet first, then record a new value for every slide position. Convolution is that process for mathematical functions, and all those recorded values form a new function.
tiers.practitioner: In practice, convolution evaluates products between one input and a reflected, shifted version of another at every shift; discrete data uses sums in place of the continuous integral. In signal and image processing, watch the reflection carefully: omitting it computes cross-correlation for real-valued inputs. The output must be evaluated across the shifts of interest, not just at one alignment.
tiers.paperLevel: For continuous functions, (f * g)(t) = integral f(tau) g(t - tau) d tau, with the integral evaluated for every shift t. Convolution is commutative, so either function may be reflected and shifted without changing the result. For real-valued functions, it differs from cross-correlation by that reflection; for complex-valued functions, the cross-correlation operator is the adjoint of the convolution operator.

explainer.example: For the discrete sequences f = [1, 2] and g = [1, 1], convolution gives [1, 3, 2]. The three values come from products at successive shifts: 1×1, then 1×1 + 2×1, then 2×1.

explainer.intuition: Convolution measures how two functions overlap as one is reflected and moved across the other. Collecting those measurements for every shift produces a new function whose shape is modified by both inputs.
howItWorks: Start with two functions, f and g.
Reflect one function about the y-axis.
Shift the reflected function by a chosen amount.
Multiply the two functions and integrate their product.
Repeat for every shift to obtain f * g.
explainer.whyItMatters: Convolution provides a common way to describe how one function modifies another through sliding overlap. That single idea supports applications across probability, statistics, acoustics, spectroscopy, signal and image processing, and vision.
misconceptions: Convolution names both the computation and the function that results from it.
It does not matter which input function is reflected and shifted; the result is commutative.
For real-valued functions, convolution and cross-correlation are not identical: convolution includes a reflection.
